text:
Gulfstream Aerospace has completed a high-altitude flight test campaign which it reports demonstrates the potential for 100% neat sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) to reduce contrail-forming particle emissions at altitudes up to 50,000ft.

The campaign marks the first flight on 100% SAF for the Gulfstream G800 and its Pearl 700 engine. The G800 flew in close formation with a specially modified Gulfstream G700, converted into a flying emissions measurement laboratory. This enabled researchers to record particulate matter and contrail-forming atmospheric characteristics at altitudes higher than most commercial airliners operate but typical for business aircraft.

The campaign was conducted in collaboration with the FAA’s Center of Excellence (ASCENT), NASA, the German Aerospace Center (DLR), Missouri University of Science and Technology, Aerodyne Research, Rolls-Royce, Montana Renewables and World Fuel Services. It was designed to isolate how fuel composition influences non-CO2 emissions.

The team compared conventional Jet A, low-sulfur Jet A and neat hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids (HEFA) SAF, which contains no sulfur or aromatics. Gulfstream said that preliminary results indicate a “significant” measurable reduction in the particulate emissions that contribute to contrail formation when operating on neat SAF.

Gulfstream’s engineering and flight test teams put in months of preparation for the study, including modifying the G700 cabin to integrate advanced inflight emissions instrumentation. Pilots trained extensively in simulators to execute complex formation profiles needed to capture both near-field emissions and contrail evolution several miles in-trail.

Mark Burns, president of Gulfstream, said: “As aviation continues its work in optimising environmental efficiencies, Gulfstream is focused on advancing solutions that deliver measurable impact today while shaping a more sustainable future for flight. This campaign reflects our strategy to lead with advanced technology, real-world testing and meaningful collaboration to better understand and reduce aviation’s environmental impact.”

Rich Moore, a research scientist at NASA, said: “This collaboration enabled these first-ever high-altitude 100% SAF emissions observations, allowing the team to operate safely and efficiently while maintaining the precision needed for accurate data collection. This real-world data is essential to improving our models and understanding aviation’s broader environmental impact.”

Julie Marks, executive director of the FAA’s Office of Environment and Energy, said: “Partnering with Gulfstream was an excellent opportunity that will help inform and quantify our efforts to mitigate the impacts of persistent contrails. We appreciate the collaboration with industry as the FAA continues to evaluate how SAF may help reduce persistent contrails.”

The data from the campaign will be utilised in partnership with the broader aviation and atmospheric science communities. It is planned that these insights will be used to help refine analytical models, inform future fuel standards and support the development of operational strategies to reduce aviation’s environmental impact.

To date, Gulfstream aircraft have flown more than 3.5 million nautical miles on SAF blends.

text:
A forestry village of 400 people in the central North Island could host New Zealand’s first integrated wood processing hub, after NZ Bio Forestry signed a heads of agreement with local iwi Ngāti Manawa to turn logs and mill residues into high-value timber, biochemicals and aviation fuel at Kaingaroa.

That is according to chief executive Wayne Mulligan, who confirmed an industrial site has been identified and is now moving through consent, with construction expected to start late this year.

“Both Murupara and Kaingaroa suffered significant economic decline,” Mulligan said, tracing the slide to the forestry reforms and privatisation of state assets that saw the NZ Forest Service shut its village operations in the late 1980s. The surrounding land was returned to iwi at the time, yet the jobs that once sustained 1,000 residents never came back.

The blueprint borrows from Scandinavia, where harvest, sawmilling, energy generation and biochemical processing routinely share a single industrial site. A wood engineering facility for high-value products would anchor the hub, feeding its residues into a biorefinery that turns out glucose bases, lactic acids and polymers bound for ethanol and sustainable aviation fuel.

Wood Central understands the village sits deep inside the Kaingaroa estate, nearly 190,000 hectares of planted radiata pine on land owned by a central North Island iwi collective and managed by Kaingaroa Tipu, the forest manager formerly known as Timberlands.

Ngāti Manawa, which represents 5,000 mana whenua across the Kaingaroa and Murupara district, has watched forestry restructuring drain the villages for more than 30 years. Chair Kani Edwards said the deal reaches past industry to jobs, skills and the prospect of whānau prospering at home rather than leaving to find work.

“If we get this right, it would be incredible,” Edwards told RNZ during the project’s feasibility stage, nominating a sawmill among the operations he wants inside the hub for a district carrying some of the highest unemployment in the Bay of Plenty.

Kaingaroa’s population now stands at 400, of whom 98 per cent are Māori, down from a peak of 1,000 three decades ago. An $11 million community development project announced in July 2024 has already delivered roading and village infrastructure upgrades ahead of any industrial build.

NZ Bio Forestry launched in 2018 with shareholders in Singapore and Taiwan and has spent eight years developing technology that converts plantation biomass into biofuels, biochemicals and biomaterials. Alongside its Taiwanese partners, the company won a Global Top 100 R&D Award for FixCarbon, a carbon-negative bioplastic derived from afforestation.

Mark Ross, chief executive of the Wood Processors and Manufacturers Association of New Zealand, welcomed the project’s scale and said the sector needs exactly this kind of regional hub, with Kaingaroa an ideal location for timber, people and transport. His endorsement follows the government naming wood processing a priority area for InvestNZ, the agency chasing investments of $100 million to $1 billion.

Capital looms as the biggest hurdle, with Mulligan conceding sovereign funds are unlikely backers because they hunt existing income streams. Funding talks span onshore and offshore investors, he said, and the money exists for anyone shown the case stacks up.

The agreement surfaces as New Zealand wood processing sheds capacity at pace, with the Juken closure at Kaitāia capping a two-year run that has stripped 570 jobs from mills including Kinleith, Eves Valley, Karioi and Tangiwai. A new-build hub would push the other way, working the same residue and low-grade log pool the Bioeconomy Science Institute says could feed a domestic bioenergy industry from seven million green tonnes a year.

Rail wagons out of the central North Island still queue for the export berths at Tauranga, yet the same port city holds proof of the other end of the chain, with the mass timber tower Mareanui claiming New Zealand’s supreme property award.

Forestry occupies 1.8 million hectares of New Zealand land compared with dairy’s 2 million yet returns a quarter of the income, Mulligan said, and Kaingaroa now shapes as the first hard test of whether wood fibre can earn more at home than it does on a log ship.

text:
India faces several threats from its rapid development, including increasing reliance on imported crude oil, worsening air pollution from agricultural residue fires, and rising greenhouse gas emissions from its aviation sector. However, India also has emerging advantages in its world-leading low-cost green hydrogen and development of large-scale agricultural residue supply chains, the report states.

New Delhi: India can turn its vast agricultural waste and low-cost green hydrogen into sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) through a power-and-biomass-to-liquids industry, according to a report co-authored by India Energy and Climate Centre, the UC Berkeley Goldman School of Public Policy, and the Energy Innovation Policy and Technology.

India faces several threats from its rapid development, including increasing reliance on imported crude oil, worsening air pollution from agricultural residue fires, and rising greenhouse gas emissions from its aviation sector. However, India also has emerging advantages in its world-leading low-cost green hydrogen and development of large-scale agricultural residue supply chains, the report states.

The Power-and-Biomass-to-Liquids ((PBtL) pathway gasifies surplus crop waste, like rice and wheat straw, and combines it with green hydrogen, converting the synthesis gas into liquid jet fuel via the Fischer-Tropsch process.

The report states that India’s PBtL route can produce SAF at costs up to roughly 40 per cent below global SAF benchmarks, driven by record-low green hydrogen prices and low agricultural residue costs.

Its results suggest that until Indian PBtL SAF can compete directly with fossil jet fuel, it can economically serve rising international SAF demand while hedging against crude oil price spikes.

The report also states that PBtL SAF has an enormous market size and could feasibly satisfy all of India’s 2050 aviation demand; that PBtL SAF production costs can fall below fossil jet fuel prices in the 2030s or earlier depending on market conditions and policy developments; and that domestic PBtL SAF has less monetary risk exposure than fossil jet fuel.

It provides a vision for how India can leverage these advantages to develop a power-and-biomass-to-liquids (PBtL) sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) industry that can deliver a domestic cost-competitive drop-in alternative to imported crude oil-dependent fossil jet fuel, create value from agricultural residue that is currently burned, and decarbonize India’s aviation sector.

The report states that PBtL is ready for commercial demonstration and growth, outcompetes other SAF technologies on cost, carbon intensity, and resource efficiency, and delivers a range of co-benefits such as avoiding premature deaths from local air pollution.

It provides a spatially detailed, district-level assessment showing that surplus agricultural residue availability and low green hydrogen costs align in the areas surrounding the Delhi, Pune, and Mumbai airports, suggesting they may be best suited for supporting the PBtL industry’s near-term growth.

The report concludes that if India can drive early investment and use smart policy to overcome first-of-a-kind deployment barriers and protect against unintended consequences, it can unlock a virtuous cycle of scale and cost reduction that boosts India’s self-reliance, public health, and global climate leadership.

title: From strategy to execution: Arlande helps build the airport of the future - Consultancy.eu
description:
“Today, airports are complex mobility hubs where operations, technology and public interests all come together.” Arlande has evolved alongside this changing landscape.
While the firm’s roots lie firmly in airport operations, its role has expanded into broader consultancy support across the entire transformation journey.
By analysing passenger flows and identifying improvement opportunities, Arlande helps airports make better-informed decisions that enhance both efficiency and the passenger experience.
As passenger volumes continue to grow, efficient baggage handling remains a critical component of airport operations.
“This strengthens our ability to address complex airport challenges from multiple perspectives,” Jasper says.
text:
Over the past decades, airports have evolved from infrastructure-driven facilities into highly complex mobility ecosystems where technology, operations, passengers and public interests intersect. That transition is far from complete. The pressure to become more sustainable, the acceleration of digitalisation and increasingly demanding passenger expectations are pushing airports to rethink how they operate.

For more than 30 years, Arlande has been helping airports navigate their next phase of change – in the Netherlands and internationally. We spoke with Jasper Wildenberg (Lead Aviation International) and Kim de Graaf (Lead Aviation in the Netherlands) about the firm’s impact and the challenges shaping the industry’s future.

“Every day, I still look at aviation with amazement,” says Jasper. “The fact that humans are capable of making such enormous objects fly remains incredible.”

Jasper has spent the past eight years working in aviation through Arlande, and describes it as one of the most fascinating industries to operate in. “Few sectors are as complex as aviation. Safety, passenger experience, logistics, technology, services and public interests all come together. Every day presents a new puzzle: how can we make the aviation system work just a little better?”

Having been with Arlande and its predecessor Bostec for almost seven years, Kim shares that perspective. “What I enjoy most is the dynamics between all the different processes and stakeholders. The challenge is bringing all these parties together around one common objective: ensuring passengers can move through the airport as efficiently and comfortably as possible.”

For passengers, the complexity behind the scenes should ideally remain invisible. Yet for those working in aviation, it is precisely that complexity that makes the sector so compelling.

“Take baggage operations, for example,” says Jasper. “Walking through the baggage basement and seeing thousands of suitcases processed every day is fascinating. A combination of hardware, software and human coordination ensures that flights can depart on time – with the right baggage.”

From operational expertise to end-to-end consultancy

Over the past three decades, the challenges facing airports have changed significantly. “Thirty years ago, the focus was primarily on infrastructure and capacity,” Jasper explains. “Today, airports are complex mobility hubs where operations, technology and public interests all come together.”

Arlande has evolved alongside this changing landscape. While the firm’s roots lie firmly in airport operations, its role has expanded into broader consultancy support across the entire transformation journey.

“We have developed into a consultancy partner that supports airports end to end – from strategy and business cases through to implementation and operational optimisation,” says Jasper. “In a complex and highly regulated sector like aviation, having both strategic insight and the ability to execute is essential.”

This combination is increasingly important as airports face a continuous need to innovate while maintaining safe and reliable operations. “Airports are constantly being challenged to become smarter, more efficient and more future-proof,” Kim says. “At the same time, they operate 24/7 and safety always comes first. Finding the right balance between innovation and operational excellence is therefore a major challenge.”

This development is also changing the role of external partners. Rather than simply delivering solutions, suppliers are increasingly expected to act as strategic partners. “The organisations that create the most value are those that are transparent, share knowledge and actively contribute to strengthening the airport organisation itself,” Kim explains.

Schiphol in Amsterdam is one of Arlande’s clients in the sector

Four priorities shaping the future of airports

To support airports in their transformation journeys, Arlande focuses on four key themes that are expected to define the sector in the years ahead.

The first is optimising passenger processes. By analysing passenger flows and identifying improvement opportunities, Arlande helps airports make better-informed decisions that enhance both efficiency and the passenger experience.

“Improving passenger flow is not only about speed,” Jasper explains. “It is about creating a smoother, more predictable journey. We have, for example, contributed to the development of the seamless flow concept and supported the testing and optimisation of self-service passport control.”

A second focus area is smart baggage. As passenger volumes continue to grow, efficient baggage handling remains a critical component of airport operations.

“We have colleagues with more than 20 years of experience in the baggage domain,” Kim says. “Their knowledge allows us to advise airports on strategic choices while also helping improve day-to-day operations through better control systems, automation and robotics.”

The third theme is innovation and sustainability – two areas that are increasingly intertwined.

“Sustainability challenges require innovation, and innovation must ultimately contribute to a more sustainable aviation system,” Jasper says. “We support airports in exploring, assessing and implementing new solutions while considering the impact on operations, the organisation and the longer term.”

One example is a project involving autonomous wheelchairs that help passengers with reduced mobility reach their departure gates. “This demonstrates how innovation is not just about technology,” Jasper explains. “It can also improve accessibility, reliability and the overall passenger experience.”

The fourth theme is integrated planning and operations: creating stronger connections between planning processes and daily execution.

“When planning and operations are better aligned, airports gain more control over disruptions, capacity challenges and operational decision-making,” Kim says. “For example, we supported the project and testing management for a temporary departure hall – a critical initiative to maintain capacity.”

Combining expertise

While each theme addresses a specific challenge, they are often closely connected. To provide a broader offering, Arlande collaborates with sister company VFM Facility Experts and DAAV, a provider of inclusive mobility solutions.

“This strengthens our ability to address complex airport challenges from multiple perspectives,” Jasper says. “VFM brings expertise in facility management, airport assets and contracts, while DAAV provides autonomous mobility solutions for passengers with reduced mobility.”

DAAV and Arlande are driving the adoption of inclusive mobility solutions at airports

The result is an integrated approach rather than a collection of separate solutions. “For clients, this means working with one coordinated team instead of multiple specialists,” Jasper explains. “Together, we can deliver solutions that work at strategic, tactical and operational levels.”

Expanding beyond the Netherlands

As aviation itself is an international industry, Arlande’s expertise is increasingly reaching beyond Dutch borders. Under Jasper’s leadership, the firm is expanding its international aviation activities, particularly around passenger and baggage processes.

“We are increasingly involved in international airport programmes,” he says. “Our experience with major European hubs allows us to quickly understand complex operational challenges and identify practical solutions.”

A key challenge facing airports, he says, is moving beyond experimentation. “Many airports remain stuck in pilots. The real challenge is making choices, setting priorities and moving towards implementation.”

One example is Arlande’s support for an international airport in developing a sourcing and operating model strategy for cleaning services. The team contributed not only sector expertise, but also support around governance and procurement. “Every airport requires a tailored approach,” Jasper explains. “Local circumstances, regulations and organisational maturity all influence what works best.”

The firm’s international ambitions are selective rather than based on the volume of projects. “Our goal is not simply to operate in as many countries as possible,” Jasper says. “We want to be active where our expertise genuinely adds value. Our ambition is to be recognised internationally as a trusted partner that combines proven airport experience with pragmatism and strong implementation capability.”

Helping airports make the right choices

In the Netherlands, Kim leads Arlande’s continued focus on supporting airports through an increasingly complex environment. “In the coming years, we want to help airports make well-informed choices about where they should invest and what will truly create value,” she says. “That is not simply about introducing new technology. It is about understanding what makes a meaningful difference today and in the future.”

Jasper agrees that successful innovation requires more than ideas. “In aviation, innovation is often not about inventing something completely new. It is about successfully scaling solutions that have already demonstrated their value,” he says. “Many airports remain in pilot mode. The real added value of consultancy lies in helping organisations make choices, prioritise and implement.”

A partner embedded in the organisation

This practical approach is central to Arlande’s identity, Kim says. “We combine deep sector expertise with practical understanding of airport processes. That means solutions are not only designed, but also implemented successfully and embraced by the organisation.”

She adds that Arlande deliberately works shoulder to shoulder with its clients. “You will not always notice us as consultants because we become part of the organisation. At the same time, we make sure knowledge is transferred and embedded. Being an independent, knowledgeable and genuinely involved partner is what defines us.”

For Kim, successful transformation ultimately comes down to collaboration. “I believe progress happens when everyone understands that they are working towards the same goal, even when different interests are involved. When we can create that shared sense of purpose across projects and organisations, that is when collaboration truly succeeds.”

Hong Kong – 10July2026 – EcoCeres, a global leader in the innovation and commercialization of renewable fuels and green molecules, announced that it will supply sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) to Viva Energy Australia (Viva Energy), one of Australia’s leading energy companies, for storage and distribution through Viva Energy’s Pinkenba fuel terminal in Brisbane, Queensland.

Under the agreement, EcoCeres’ SAF will be delivered to Viva Energy’s Pinkenba facility, which has recently been upgraded to store, blend and handle SAF alongside conventional jet fuel. From Pinkenba, Viva Energy will be able to supply blended SAF to its aviation customers, supporting the development of a lower‑carbon fuel supply chain for the Australian aviation market.

EcoCeres produces SAF from 100% waste‑based feedstocks, such as used cooking oil and other waste lipids, which can deliver significant lifecycle greenhouse‑gas emissions reductions of up to 94.4% compared with conventional jet fuel. Viva Energy’s Pinkenba SAF infrastructure project, supported by funding from the Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA), has been designed to demonstrate the delivery of SAF through existing fuel supply infrastructure to Brisbane Airport and beyond.

Matti Lievonen, CEO of EcoCeres said: “Partnering with Viva Energy to further expand the availability of our SAF in the Australian market is an important milestone in EcoCeres’ growth journey and in the broader decarbonization of aviation in this region. By supplying SAF to Viva Energy, we are able to connect our production capabilities with established storage and distribution infrastructure, helping airlines access low‑carbon fuel at scale through familiar supply chains.” He added, “Australia is a key growth market for sustainable fuels, and we look forward to working with Viva Energy and its customers to turn net‑zero ambitions into concrete emissions reductions in the years ahead.”

The collaboration between EcoCeres and Viva Energy will help lay the foundation for a more mature SAF ecosystem in Australia by demonstrating how existing terminal infrastructure can be used for SAF storage, blending and distribution, while providing airlines with access to certified waste‑based SAF without requiring changes to aircraft or airport refueling infrastructure, and creating a platform for future initiatives such as book‑and‑claim systems and broader regional supply chains for low‑carbon liquid fuels.

text:
Overview

The global aircraft fuel systems market was valued at US$ 9.7 billion in 2025 and is expected to reach US$ 12.5 billion by 2033, growing at a CAGR of 3.1% during the forecast period 2026–2033. Aircraft fuel systems are critical to aircraft performance and safety, comprising integrated components such as fuel tanks, pumps, valves, filters, pipelines, sensors, fuel quantity indication systems, and fuel management technologies that ensure the safe storage, transfer, monitoring, and delivery of fuel to aircraft engines. As airlines and aircraft manufacturers continue to prioritize fuel efficiency, operational reliability, and lifecycle cost reduction, demand is increasing for more intelligent fuel management systems capable of supporting digital monitoring, predictive maintenance, and optimized fuel utilization. The aviation industry's broader digital transformation is also accelerating the adoption of standardized fuel data management and analytics to improve operational efficiency throughout the fuel supply chain and aircraft operations. Recent initiatives such as the International Air Transport Association's (IATA) FuelIS analytics platform and Fuel Data Standards further demonstrate the industry's increasing focus on digital fuel management and operational optimization.

The market is also being reshaped by the rapid expansion of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) adoption as airlines, aircraft manufacturers, and governments pursue long-term decarbonization goals. Although SAF is designed as a drop-in fuel compatible with existing aircraft, its growing commercial deployment is driving additional validation, testing, certification, and optimization of aircraft fuel handling, storage, metering, and monitoring systems to ensure reliable operation across a wider range of approved fuel blends. According to IATA, sustainable aviation fuel is expected to contribute approximately 65% of the emissions reductions required for aviation to achieve net-zero carbon emissions by 2050, reinforcing continued investment in SAF-compatible aircraft technologies and supporting infrastructure.

Beyond SAF, aircraft manufacturers and aerospace suppliers are accelerating research into next-generation propulsion technologies, particularly liquid hydrogen-powered aircraft, which require fundamentally different fuel storage, transfer, thermal management, and pressure control systems compared with conventional aviation fuels. Reflecting this long-term transition, Airbus, Parker Hannifin, Marshall, and GKN Aerospace announced collaborations during 2024 to advance hydrogen fuel system technologies through the HyFIVE consortium, supporting the development of zero-emission aircraft expected in the next decade. While hydrogen aviation remains at an early stage of commercialization, continued investment in advanced fuel system architectures is expanding innovation opportunities and strengthening the long-term outlook for the global aircraft fuel systems market.

Drivers

Rising Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) Adoption Driving Demand for Compatible Aircraft Fuel Systems

The increasing adoption of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) is a major driver for the aircraft fuel systems market as the aviation industry accelerates efforts to reduce lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions while continuing to utilize existing aircraft fleets. Although SAF is approved as a drop-in replacement for conventional jet fuel within certified blending limits, expanding its commercial use requires extensive qualification of aircraft fuel management systems, fuel pumps, valves, seals, filters, fuel quantity indication systems, and fuel control components to ensure long-term compatibility, material integrity, and operational reliability. Aircraft OEMs and fuel system manufacturers are therefore investing in component validation, testing, and certification programs to support increasing SAF utilization across commercial and military aviation.

Commercial deployment of SAF continues to accelerate globally. According to the International Air Transport Association (IATA), global SAF production is expected to reach approximately 2 million tonnes (around 2.5 billion litres) in 2025, representing more than a two-fold increase compared with 2024 production. Although this still accounts for less than 1% of total global aviation fuel consumption, the rapid expansion in production capacity is encouraging airlines and aircraft manufacturers to prepare fleets for broader SAF adoption through continued investment in compatible aircraft fuel system technologies.

Aircraft manufacturers are also progressing toward higher SAF utilization. Airbus has stated that all of its commercial aircraft are currently certified to operate using up to 50% SAF blends and is working with engine manufacturers and fuel suppliers to support operation using 100% SAF before 2030. As airlines progressively increase SAF usage to meet decarbonization commitments and regulatory targets, demand for advanced aircraft fuel management systems, fuel distribution systems, fuel monitoring systems, and high-performance fuel handling components is expected to grow steadily throughout the forecast period.

Growing Aircraft Production and Fleet Modernization Supporting OEM and Aftermarket Demand

Growing commercial aircraft production and fleet modernization programs are significantly driving demand for aircraft fuel systems across both OEM and aftermarket channels. Airlines worldwide are replacing older aircraft with more fuel-efficient platforms that incorporate advanced aircraft fuel management systems, lightweight fuel tanks, digitally integrated fuel quantity indication systems, fuel monitoring technologies, and high-efficiency fuel pumps and valves. These next-generation systems improve operational reliability, optimize fuel consumption, and reduce maintenance requirements while supporting compliance with increasingly stringent aviation safety and environmental standards.

The industry's exceptionally large aircraft backlog provides strong long-term visibility for fuel system suppliers. According to Airbus, the company reported a commercial aircraft backlog exceeding 8,700 aircraft at the end of 2025, while Boeing's commercial backlog remained above 6,000 aircraft. Every new aircraft delivered requires complete fuel storage, transfer, monitoring, filtration, and control systems, creating sustained demand for aircraft fuel system manufacturers throughout the production lifecycle.

Beyond new aircraft production, the expanding global fleet is generating substantial recurring revenue through aftermarket maintenance, repair, and overhaul (MRO) activities. Aircraft fuel pumps, valves, sensors, filters, fuel lines, and fuel quantity indication systems require periodic inspection, replacement, calibration, and certification throughout an aircraft's operational life. As global passenger traffic continues to recover and airlines increase aircraft utilization, demand for aftermarket aircraft fuel system components and MRO services is expected to remain a major contributor to long-term market growth.

Restraint

Lengthy Certification Requirements and Complex Aerospace Supply Chains

Lengthy certification processes and complex aerospace supply chains remain significant restraints on the aircraft fuel systems market. Aircraft fuel systems are classified as safety-critical equipment and therefore must comply with rigorous certification requirements established by aviation authorities including the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA), and other national regulators. New fuel pumps, valves, sensors, electronic fuel management systems, and integrated fuel control components must undergo extensive laboratory qualification, environmental testing, vibration testing, electromagnetic compatibility assessment, flight validation, and reliability demonstration before receiving airworthiness approval. These extensive validation procedures increase development costs and extend commercialization timelines for new technologies.

The market is further constrained by dependence on highly specialized aerospace suppliers that manufacture precision valves, sensors, actuators, electronic controllers, filtration systems, and advanced sealing materials. Supply disruptions affecting titanium, nickel alloys, electronic components, and aerospace-grade castings continue to extend lead times for aircraft production and replacement parts. According to Airbus' 2025 Full-Year Results, persistent supply chain challenges remained one of the principal factors affecting aircraft production and delivery schedules, illustrating how upstream manufacturing constraints continue to influence demand across the broader aircraft fuel systems supply chain.

Aircraft Fuel Systems Market Trends & Opportunities

Digital Aircraft Fuel Management and Predictive Health Monitoring

Digitalization is emerging as a major trend across the aircraft fuel systems market as airlines increasingly adopt intelligent aircraft fuel management systems capable of improving operational efficiency, maintenance planning, and fuel utilization. Modern aircraft fuel systems increasingly integrate electronic sensors, fuel quantity indication systems, flow monitoring devices, and onboard diagnostics that provide continuous operational data to flight crews and maintenance teams. These technologies enable predictive maintenance, reduce unscheduled component failures, improve fuel efficiency, and enhance aircraft dispatch reliability while lowering lifecycle operating costs.

Supporting this trend, the International Air Transport Association (IATA) continues to expand its FuelIS platform and Fuel Data Standards, enabling airlines to analyze fuel consumption, benchmark operational performance, and identify fuel-saving opportunities using standardized digital data. As airlines continue investing in digital fleet management and operational analytics, demand for intelligent aircraft fuel monitoring systems and digitally connected fuel management technologies is expected to increase steadily.

Hydrogen Propulsion Accelerating Innovation in Next-Generation Aircraft Fuel Systems

The growing development of hydrogen-powered aircraft is driving innovation in next-generation aircraft fuel systems capable of handling cryogenic liquid hydrogen and other zero-emission propulsion technologies. Unlike conventional jet fuel, liquid hydrogen requires specialized storage tanks, advanced thermal insulation, pressure regulation systems, cryogenic valves, and highly sophisticated fuel transfer technologies. These engineering requirements are encouraging aerospace manufacturers to redesign aircraft fuel system architectures for future aircraft platforms.

Industry collaboration continues to accelerate technology development. In 2024, Parker Aerospace joined Marshall, GKN Aerospace, and other partners within the HyFIVE consortium to develop liquid hydrogen fuel system technologies supporting future zero-emission aviation. Although hydrogen-powered commercial aircraft remain under development, these investments are expanding research into advanced aircraft fuel tanks, cryogenic fuel management systems, thermal control technologies, and next-generation fuel distribution systems, creating long-term opportunities for suppliers across the aircraft fuel systems market.

Segment Analysis

The global aircraft fuel systems industry is segmented based on system, technology, engine type, aircraft type, point of sale and by region.

Fleet Expansion and Aircraft Modernization Sustain Commercial Aviation Leadership

The commercial aviation segment accounted for approximately 56.4% of the global aircraft fuel systems market in 2025, making it the largest aircraft type segment. Its dominance is supported by continuous fleet expansion, rising aircraft production, and sustained investments in fuel-efficient commercial aircraft. Aircraft fuel systems—including fuel tanks, fuel pumps, valves, fuel quantity indication systems, fuel management systems, and fuel distribution networks—are essential for ensuring safe fuel storage, accurate fuel monitoring, efficient fuel transfer, and reliable engine performance throughout flight operations. Airlines are increasingly adopting advanced aircraft fuel systems that improve fuel efficiency, reduce maintenance requirements, and support compatibility with sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).

Long-term aircraft production forecasts continue to reinforce demand for OEM aircraft fuel systems. According to Airbus' Global Market Forecast 2024, approximately 42,430 new passenger and freighter aircraft will be required globally by 2043. Similarly, Boeing's Commercial Market Outlook 2024 projects demand for over 43,900 new commercial airplanes during the same period. Continued aircraft deliveries, fleet replacement programs, increasing passenger traffic, and growing adoption of digital fuel management technologies are expected to sustain commercial aviation's leadership throughout the forecast period.

Global Defense Modernization Programs Fuel Military Aviation Growth

Military aviation is projected to register the fastest growth throughout the forecast period owing to increasing defense modernization programs, rising procurement of fighter aircraft, transport aircraft, helicopters, and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). Modern military platforms require highly specialized aircraft fuel systems capable of operating under extreme temperatures, high-G maneuvers, aerial refueling operations, and extended mission durations while maintaining operational reliability and aircraft survivability.

According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), global military expenditure reached a record US$2.72 trillion in 2024, representing a 9.4% increase compared with 2023. Rising defense budgets are accelerating investments in next-generation combat aircraft equipped with lightweight fuel tanks, crash-resistant fuel storage systems, digital fuel monitoring, and advanced fuel tank inerting technologies. These modernization initiatives are expected to significantly increase demand for advanced military aircraft fuel systems.

Large Installed Aircraft Fleet Continues to Support Conventional Engine Dominance

Conventional engines accounted for approximately 95% of the aircraft fuel systems market in 2025 due to the extensive global fleet of turbofan, turboprop, turboshaft, and piston-powered aircraft. Commercial airlines, military operators, business aviation fleets, and regional carriers continue to rely primarily on conventional propulsion systems supported by mature aircraft fuel management technologies.

Although hybrid-electric propulsion is gaining industry attention, the overwhelming majority of new aircraft deliveries during the forecast period are expected to utilize conventional engines. Their established certification standards, global maintenance infrastructure, and proven operational reliability continue to sustain demand for conventional aircraft fuel systems across both OEM and aftermarket channels. Hybrid-electric aircraft remain primarily in demonstration and developmental phases, limiting current commercial revenue contribution.

Next-Generation Aircraft Propulsion Technologies Drive Hybrid-Electric Adoption

Hybrid-electric propulsion is expected to be the fastest-growing engine segment as the aviation industry accelerates development of lower-emission aircraft technologies. Aircraft manufacturers are actively evaluating hybrid-electric propulsion architectures to improve fuel efficiency, reduce greenhouse gas emissions, and support future sustainability objectives.

Programs such as Airbus' ZEROe initiative and multiple regional aircraft demonstration projects are driving development of integrated fuel management systems capable of supporting both conventional fuel and electric propulsion technologies. As hybrid-electric aircraft progress toward commercialization, demand for next-generation aircraft fuel systems with advanced control, monitoring, and energy management capabilities is expected to grow steadily.

Increasing Focus on Fuel Efficiency and System Reliability Sustains Fuel Supply & Distribution Leadership

Fuel Supply & Distribution Systems represented approximately 43% of the global aircraft fuel systems market in 2025. This segment includes fuel pumps, valves, fuel injectors, filters, pipelines, hoses, and associated fuel control components responsible for delivering fuel safely and efficiently to aircraft engines under varying flight conditions.

The segment continues to benefit from increasing aircraft production, fleet modernization, and growing emphasis on operational efficiency. Aircraft manufacturers are investing in lightweight fuel distribution systems, digitally monitored fuel flow technologies, and improved fuel control architectures that enhance aircraft performance while supporting compatibility with sustainable aviation fuels.

Enhanced Aircraft Safety Standards Accelerate Fuel Tank Inerting System Deployment

Fuel Tank Inerting Systems are projected to witness the fastest growth during the forecast period owing to increasing emphasis on aircraft safety and regulatory compliance. These systems reduce oxygen concentration inside aircraft fuel tanks through nitrogen-enriched air generation, significantly minimizing ignition risk during flight operations.

Growing integration of inert gas generation systems into commercial aircraft, military aircraft, and next-generation aviation platforms is supporting market growth. Continued emphasis on flight safety, fuel tank explosion prevention, and evolving aircraft certification requirements is expected to accelerate adoption of advanced fuel tank inerting technologies worldwide.

Reliable Fuel Delivery Across Modern Aircraft Platforms Supports Pump Feed System Dominance

Pump Feed Systems accounted for approximately 68% of the aircraft fuel systems market in 2025 due to their widespread deployment across commercial aircraft, military aircraft, helicopters, and business jets. These systems provide consistent fuel pressure regardless of aircraft attitude, altitude, or maneuvering conditions, making them indispensable for modern turbine-powered aircraft.

Increasing aircraft production, growing fleet utilization, and continuous improvements in fuel pump efficiency, reliability, and digital monitoring capabilities continue to strengthen demand for pump feed systems across both OEM and replacement markets.

Geographical Penetration

North America Aircraft Fuel Systems Market: Driven by SAF Commercialization and Advanced Aircraft Development

North America accounted for approximately 43.2% of the global aircraft fuel systems market in 2025, supported by its strong aircraft manufacturing ecosystem, continuous investment in aviation technologies, and leadership in sustainable aviation initiatives. The region is home to major aircraft OEMs, engine manufacturers, and aircraft system suppliers, creating sustained demand for advanced aircraft fuel systems, fuel management systems, fuel pumps, valves, sensors, and fuel monitoring technologies across both commercial and military aviation.

Government policy continues to strengthen market growth. The U.S. Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) Grand Challenge targets production of 3 billion gallons of SAF annually by 2030 and 35 billion gallons by 2050, accelerating industry investment in SAF-compatible aircraft fuel systems. At the same time, manufacturers are preparing for future propulsion technologies. In April 2024, Parker Aerospace joined the HyFIVE consortium to support development of liquid hydrogen fuel systems for next-generation aircraft, reinforcing North America's position as a leading center for aircraft fuel system innovation. Combined with strong MRO activity, aircraft fleet renewal, and continued commercial aircraft production, these factors continue to drive the regional aircraft fuel systems market.

Europe Aircraft Fuel Systems Market: Driven by Aviation Decarbonization and Next-Generation Propulsion Innovation

Europe represents a significant aircraft fuel systems market owing to ambitious decarbonization policies, continuous aerospace innovation, and increasing investment in sustainable aircraft technologies. Aircraft manufacturers, engine suppliers, and system integrators across the region are accelerating development of fuel-efficient aircraft platforms while advancing aircraft fuel management systems capable of supporting sustainable aviation fuels and future hydrogen-powered aircraft.

The European Union continues to strengthen aviation decarbonization through ReFuelEU Aviation, which mandates increasing SAF supply at EU airports beginning in 2025 and progressively raising blending requirements through 2050. These regulatory measures are encouraging airlines, OEMs, and fuel system manufacturers to accelerate development of SAF-compatible aircraft fuel tanks, pumps, valves, fuel metering units, and monitoring systems. Alongside SAF adoption, European aerospace companies continue investing in hydrogen aircraft research, digital aircraft systems, and lightweight fuel storage technologies, supporting long-term growth of the aircraft fuel systems industry.

Asia-Pacific Aircraft Fuel Systems Market: Driven by Record Aircraft Deliveries and Expanding Aerospace Manufacturing

Asia-Pacific is projected to register the fastest growth during the forecast period, driven by rapidly expanding commercial aviation, rising defense procurement, and increasing domestic aerospace manufacturing capabilities. Rising passenger traffic, expanding airline fleets, and growing aircraft production are generating substantial demand for aircraft fuel systems, fuel distribution systems, fuel pumps, aircraft fuel tanks, and advanced fuel monitoring technologies.

According to Airbus' Global Market Forecast 2024, Asia-Pacific will account for the largest share of global aircraft deliveries over the next two decades as airlines continue expanding capacity to meet rising passenger demand. India and China are also investing heavily in indigenous aerospace manufacturing while strengthening commercial aviation infrastructure. At the same time, countries including Japan, South Korea, Australia, and India continue modernizing military aircraft fleets, increasing demand for advanced military aircraft fuel systems, crash-resistant fuel tanks, and fuel tank inerting technologies. Growing aircraft production, expanding MRO infrastructure, and increasing OEM investment are expected to sustain strong regional growth.

South America Aircraft Fuel Systems Market: Supported by Fleet Renewal and Expanding Commercial Aviation

The South America aircraft fuel systems market is experiencing steady growth as airlines modernize aging fleets and regional air travel continues recovering. Commercial aircraft operators across Brazil, Chile, Colombia, and Argentina are investing in newer fuel-efficient aircraft that require advanced aircraft fuel systems capable of improving operational efficiency while supporting future sustainable aviation fuel adoption.

Brazil continues to strengthen its position as the region's aerospace manufacturing hub through Embraer's commercial, executive, and defense aircraft production. In parallel, governments and airlines are increasing investment in aviation infrastructure and fleet modernization programs to improve connectivity across the continent. Growing aircraft deliveries, increasing maintenance activities, and expanding aftermarket demand for aircraft fuel pumps, valves, filters, sensors, and fuel management systems are expected to support continued growth of the South American aircraft fuel systems market.

Middle East & Africa Aircraft Fuel Systems Market: Driven by Airline Expansion and Military Aviation Investments

The Middle East & Africa aircraft fuel systems market is growing steadily due to ongoing airline fleet expansion, increasing defense aviation investments, and continued development of regional aviation infrastructure. Leading Middle Eastern airlines continue investing in next-generation commercial aircraft to support long-haul international operations, generating demand for advanced aircraft fuel systems, fuel management systems, fuel quantity indication systems, and fuel distribution technologies.

The region also remains a major defense aviation market, with countries including Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Qatar investing in advanced fighter aircraft, transport aircraft, helicopters, and military support platforms. According to SIPRI, the Middle East remains one of the world's highest defense spending regions relative to GDP, supporting sustained procurement of modern military aircraft equipped with sophisticated fuel storage, fuel transfer, and fuel monitoring systems. Simultaneously, expansion of regional MRO capabilities and increasing adoption of fuel-efficient aircraft are expected to strengthen long-term demand for aircraft fuel systems across the Middle East & Africa.

Key Developments

·In April 2026, Eaton signed an agreement with Air Support to provide local repair and support for Eaton’s engine fuel components for large commercial aircraft. Under the agreement, Air Support became the first authorized service center for Eaton’s aerospace business across Europe, the Middle East, and Africa, significantly expanding Eaton’s aftermarket fuel system service network and improving maintenance accessibility for commercial aircraft operators across the region.

·In March 2025, the first sustainable aviation fuels (SAF) delivery took place at the Airbus Canada's A220 site, enabling the Mirabel teams to use SAF for production, customer acceptance and test flights. This now means that all Airbus commercial aircraft assembly sites around the world are now using sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) for their internal operations. During the course of 2025, all Airbus commercial aircraft delivery centers around the world will offer SAF to customers for ferry flights. This year alone, in 2025, over 600,000 litres of SAF with a 30% blend are expected to be used at the Airbus Mirabel site resulting in a reduction in CO2 emissions of around 400 metric tons.

text: Which companies actually need sustainable aviation fuel certificates (SAFc)? The primary candidates are companies with aviation footprints, typically from business travel, upstream freight, and downstream freight. That means two profiles: large, multi-national companies where travel is integral to the business (consultancies, technology companies, law firms, financial services), and companies moving goods by air (pharma, high-value manufacturing, logistics providers). Companies with validated SBTi targets are also especially strong candidates. SBTi’s final Corporate Net-Zero Standard V.0 (June 2026) formally recognises book-and-claim SAFc as counting toward Scope 3 targets, reported transparently alongside the inventory rather than subtracted from it. That recognition reflects what SAF actually does: fund physical lower carbon fuel that displaces fossil kerosene, cutting emissions at the source rather than compensating for them elsewhere. The GHG Protocol doesn't yet take an explicit position on whether SAFc reduces your gross reported footprint. 𝗖𝗹𝗶𝗺𝗲𝗙𝗶 𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻: Engage your carbon auditors early. SAFc can demonstrate progress toward an SBTi target; whether it should also reduce a GHG-protocol audited footprint is less settled. It is often left to auditors, and practice varies. One clean way through is dual accounting: report the footprint both with and without SAFc, and be fully transparent about the assumptions behind each number. Full details on eligibility, accounting, and how to structure a first SAFc purchase can be found in our recent publication: ‘SAF Certificates: A Buyer’s Guide’. title: ASA Calls for EPA Review of Soybean Oil Renewable Diesel RFS Pathway - Grain Journal
description:
ASA contends that while soybean oil is an approved feedstock for renewable diesel, biodiesel, sustainable aviation fuel and heating oil, renewable naphtha and renewable liquefied petroleum gas produced from soybean oil are not eligible to generate RINs.
According to ASA, the difference stems from EPA's original lifecycle analysis for soybean oil renewable diesel, which relied on a displacement accounting method when evaluating greenhouse gas emissions.
The organization said expanding eligibility would increase the value of soybean oil for renewable diesel producers and improve returns throughout the supply chain.
Using an illustrative production scenario, ASA estimated that renewable diesel output consists of approximately 91 percent renewable diesel, 4.5 percent renewable naphtha, 3.5 percent renewable LPG and 1 percent unrecovered fuel gas.
ASA said doing so would align soybean oil treatment with comparable renewable fuel pathways under the Renewable Fuel Standard.
text:
The American Soybean Association is urging the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to update its lifecycle analysis for soybean oil used in renewable diesel production, arguing that current Renewable Fuel Standard accounting methods place soybean oil at a competitive disadvantage compared with other approved feedstocks.

The organization said the Renewable Fuel Standard, established in 2005 and expanded in 2007, has been a key driver of investment in renewable fuels by requiring increasing volumes of biofuels in the nation's fuel supply. Compliance with the program relies on Renewable Identification Numbers, or RINs, which are generated when qualifying renewable fuels are produced and later blended into transportation fuels.

ASA contends that while soybean oil is an approved feedstock for renewable diesel, biodiesel, sustainable aviation fuel and heating oil, renewable naphtha and renewable liquefied petroleum gas produced from soybean oil are not eligible to generate RINs. Comparable co-products produced from other commercial fats and oils, including canola oil, distillers corn oil, sorghum oil and used cooking oil, can qualify for credits under current EPA approvals.

According to ASA, the difference stems from EPA's original lifecycle analysis for soybean oil renewable diesel, which relied on a displacement accounting method when evaluating greenhouse gas emissions. Under that approach, renewable naphtha and LPG are treated as substitutes for petroleum products rather than renewable fuels with their own share of process emissions. As a result, the co-products do not qualify for RIN generation.

The association said the methodology was adopted when renewable diesel technology and indirect land use change modeling were still developing, creating significant uncertainty in the original analysis.

ASA said updated modeling indicates soybean oil renewable diesel and its co-products can meet the Renewable Fuel Standard's requirement of at least a 50 percent reduction in greenhouse gas emissions compared with fossil fuels when an energy allocation approach is used. Under that method, renewable naphtha and LPG produced from soybean oil would be eligible for D4 RINs in the same manner as comparable co-products from other approved feedstocks.

The organization said expanding eligibility would increase the value of soybean oil for renewable diesel producers and improve returns throughout the supply chain.

Using an illustrative production scenario, ASA estimated that renewable diesel output consists of approximately 91 percent renewable diesel, 4.5 percent renewable naphtha, 3.5 percent renewable LPG and 1 percent unrecovered fuel gas. Based on assumed production yields and a RIN price of $2.06, the association calculated that the inability to generate RINs for soybean oil co-products represents about 23 cents per gallon of renewable diesel in lost value, equivalent to roughly 33 cents per bushel of soybeans if the value were passed back to producers.

ASA acknowledged that actual values would vary depending on market conditions, production yields and facility operations but said the exclusion of soybean oil co-products reduces the overall value refiners can capture from soybean-based renewable diesel.

The association is asking EPA to revisit the assumptions used in its original soybean oil renewable diesel analysis by incorporating updated lifecycle data, current production performance and a co-product accounting approach consistent with that used for similar feedstocks. ASA said doing so would align soybean oil treatment with comparable renewable fuel pathways under the Renewable Fuel Standard.

title: EIA maintains 2026 production forecasts for renewable diesel, SAF in July STEO
description:
The outlook for 2026 biodiesel production was revised down.
The EIA currently expects renewable diesel production to average 240,000 barrels per day in 2026 and 290,000 barrels per day in 2027.
Renewable diesel production averaged 190,000 barrels per day last year.
The EIA maintained its forecast that net imports of renewable diesel will average 10,000 barrels per day next year.
The EIA maintained its forecast for 2026 and 2027 renewable diesel consumption at 220,000 barrels per day and 300,000 barrels per day, respectively.
text:
The U.S. Energy Information Administration maintained its 2026 production forecasts for renewable diesel and a category of fuel that includes sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) in its latest Short-Term Energy Outlook, released July 7. The outlook for 2026 biodiesel production was revised down.

The EIA currently expects renewable diesel production to average 240,000 barrels per day in 2026 and 290,000 barrels per day in 2027. Both forecasts were maintained from the June STEO. Renewable diesel production averaged 190,000 barrels per day last year.

Net imports of renewable diesel are currently expected to average -20,000 barrels per day this year, compared to last month’s forecast of –10,000 barrels per day. The EIA maintained its forecast that net imports of renewable diesel will average 10,000 barrels per day next year. Net imports of renewable diesel were at -30,000 barrels per day in 2025.

The EIA maintained its forecast for 2026 and 2027 renewable diesel consumption at 220,000 barrels per day and 300,000 barrels per day, respectively. Renewable diesel consumption was at 160,000 barrels per day last year.

The agency now expects biodiesel production to average 100,000 barrels per day in 2026, down from last month’s forecast of 110,000 barrels per day. The EIA, however, maintained its forecast that biodiesel production will average 110,000 barrels per day in 2027. Biodiesel production averaged 80,000 barrels per day in 2025.

The EIA expects net imports of biodiesel to be at zero this year, expanding to 10,000 barrels per day next year. Both forecasts were maintained from the June STEO. Net imports of biodiesel were at zero last year.

The agency currently expects biodiesel consumption to average 100,000 barrels per day this year and 110,000 barrels per day next year, down from last month’s respective forecasts of 110,000 barrels per day and 120,000 barrels per day. Biodiesel consumption averaged 70,000 barrels per day in 2025.

The production of “other biofuel,” defined to include renewable heating oil; renewable jet fuel, including sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), alternative jet fuel, and biojet; renewable naphtha renewable gasoline and other emerging biofuels that are in various stages of development, is currently expected to average 40,000 barrels per day in 2026 and 50,000 barrels per day in 2027. Both forecasts were unchanged when compared to last month. The production of “other biofuels” was at 40,000 barrels per day in 2025.

Net imports of “other biofuel” are expected to be zero in both 2026 and 2027, unchanged from last month’s forecast and the volume of net imports reported for 2025.

The EIA maintained its forecast that consumption of “other biofuel” would average 40,000 barrels per day this year and 50,000 barrels per day next year. Consumption of “other biofuel” was at 40,000 barrels per day last year.

text:
The 3rd BRICS Transport Working Group (TWG) Meeting commenced in Nagpur today under India's BRICS Chairship 2026, bringing together senior officials from BRICS Member Countries to advance cooperation on sustainable, resilient and future-ready transport systems.

Over the next two days, the delegates will deliberate on key policy priorities covering sustainable transport infrastructure, clean mobility, logistics resilience and multimodal connectivity, while strengthening institutional cooperation to address emerging global transport challenges.

Welcoming the delegates, Secretary, Ministry of Road Transport & Highways, Shri V. Umashankar, reaffirmed India's commitment to collaborative and inclusive development guided by the timeless principle of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam—the world is one family.

He said India's BRICS Chairship theme, "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability," embodies a people-centric vision that seeks practical partnerships for creating efficient, sustainable and resilient transport ecosystems.

Highlighting the priorities of India's Chairship, the Secretary said the transport agenda has been structured around six flagship initiatives focusing on sustainability in infrastructure, sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), transport decarbonisation, urban mobility, resilient logistics and railway research cooperation. These initiatives aim to deepen knowledge sharing, encourage technical collaboration, strengthen institutional partnerships and support capacity building across BRICS Member Countries.

He observed that the proposed initiatives build upon the progress achieved during previous BRICS Transport Working Group engagements while laying a stronger foundation for long-term cooperation in the sector. Collectively, they reflect the shared commitment of BRICS nations to developing transport systems that are innovative, environmentally responsible and responsive to the aspirations of people.

Shri V. Umashankar noted that the Nagpur meeting marks the culmination of an extensive consultative process involving five virtual preparatory meetings, during which Member Countries engaged in detailed discussions on the priority thematic areas identified under India's Chairship. Appreciating the constructive participation of all delegations, he expressed confidence that the same spirit of cooperation would guide the deliberations and help build broad consensus on key outcomes.

Reaffirming India's role as Chair, he assured participating delegations that the discussions would remain transparent, inclusive and consensus-driven, ensuring that the outcomes reflect the collective priorities and development perspectives of all BRICS Members.

He also underlined the growing significance of the expanded BRICS grouping, noting that its Member Countries together account for 49.5 per cent of the world's population, 40 per cent of global GDP and 26 per cent of global trade. In this context, he said enhanced cooperation in transport has the potential to strengthen connectivity, improve supply-chain resilience and contribute meaningfully to sustainable economic growth.

The Secretary expressed confidence that the deliberations over the next two days would reinforce the spirit of partnership and mutual learning among BRICS nations and pave the way for substantive outcomes at the forthcoming Ministerial Meeting.

The Working Group Meeting will be followed by the 3rd BRICS Transport Ministers' Meeting, scheduled to be held in Nagpur on 11th July 2026.

text:
SOCAR Türkiye and Pegasus Take a Strategic Cooperation Step in Sustainable Aviation Fuel

(SOCAR) SOCAR Türkiye and Pegasus Airlines have signed a cooperation agreement in the field of Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF). The agreement between the parties establishes an important foundation for supporting sustainability-driven transformation in the energy and aviation sectors.

Under the agreement signed between SOCAR Türkiye and Pegasus Airlines, the two organizations aim to work together on identifying SAF-related needs in Türkiye, conducting feasibility studies for the development of the SAF value chain, implementing business development and awareness activities, and evaluating cooperation opportunities related to sustainable aviation fuels in Türkiye and other geographies.

SOCAR Türkiye, Türkiye's largest integrated industrial group, is carrying out work focused on innovation and new energy solutions in the areas of SAF production, supply chain, and technological partnerships, while Pegasus Airlines, an airline operating on a global scale, aims to contribute to the process by determining market needs for SAF usage and through its knowledge and experience regarding the effective use of SAF in the aviation fuel value chain.

SOCAR Türkiye CEO Elchin Ibadov, emphasizing that sustainability is one of SOCAR Türkiye’s strategic priorities, stated:

“As SOCAR Türkiye, we view energy transformation as a long-term responsibility and place great importance on developing new cooperation models with a focus on sustainability. While sustainable aviation fuels play a critical role in reducing the aviation sector’s carbon footprint, we value working alongside strong and visionary stakeholders in this field. This agreement we have signed with Pegasus represents an important step toward evaluating Türkiye’s potential in sustainable aviation fuels and addressing future cooperation opportunities. We believe this process will produce results that create value for our sectors and our country.”

Pegasus Airlines CEO Güliz Öztürk, in her remarks, drew attention to the importance of using sustainable fuels in the aviation sector and stated:

The future of aviation can only be shaped with confidence when sustainable solutions are pursued with determination. As Pegasus, we have long supported this transformation through our young fleet, our operational efficiency programs, and our medium- and long-term carbon emission reduction strategy. Since 2022, we have been using SAF in increasing volumes and across a wider geography. This agreement we have signed with SOCAR Türkiye will allow us to further deepen our expertise in sustainable aviation fuels while contributing to the development of the SAF ecosystem in Türkiye. We see this cooperation as a strategic step toward both better understanding the sector’s needs and uncovering new opportunities for the clean aviation of the future.

title: Beyond Storage: How Captured Carbon Can Be Utilized - Bipartisan Policy Center
description:
Carbon capture technologies can be grouped into two general buckets: carbon dioxide removal and point-source carbon capture.
Carbon dioxide removal (CDR) refers to a suite of practices that directly remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, including direct air capture (DAC), bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS), enhanced rock weathering, marine CDR, and others.
Carbon utilization is the repurposing of captured carbon for the production of valuable products and materials.
Applying EOR with carbon dioxide can result in net emissions reductions compared to conventional oil production as the injected carbon dioxide ultimately remains in the underground reservoir, a form of secure storage.
Carbon dioxide, either captured carbon or the collected byproduct carbon dioxide, can be injected into concrete during the mixing process.
text:
Carbon dioxide is an important feedstock for existing and novel industrial and commercial applications. Public and private efforts to reduce atmospheric concentrations of carbon dioxide to mitigate climate change can result in the capture of significant volumes of carbon dioxide. Putting this captured carbon to use—displacing carbon dioxide that is currently extracted from underground deposits—can strengthen domestic supply chains and support U.S. energy security while delivering environmental benefits. With the global carbon capture and utilization industry expected to grow significantly, federal support to scale the domestic carbon capture sector can help meet industrial demand for carbon dioxide and ensure that U.S. companies remain competitive.

How is Carbon Captured?

Carbon capture technologies can be grouped into two general buckets: carbon dioxide removal and point-source carbon capture.

Carbon dioxide removal (CDR) refers to a suite of practices that directly remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, including direct air capture (DAC), bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS), enhanced rock weathering, marine CDR, and others.

Point-source carbon capture refers to the capture of carbon emissions directly from industrial sources such as a coal or natural gas power plant or ethanol facility.

Some CDR pathways and point-source carbon capture technologies yield a stream of carbon dioxide (with varying levels of purity), which can then be stored permanently or used.

What is Carbon Utilization?

Carbon utilization is the repurposing of captured carbon for the production of valuable products and materials. Global industry currently uses around 230 million tons of carbon dioxide each year, according to the International Energy Agency. Currently, most industrial users rely on carbon dioxide that is extracted from natural underground deposits and piped to the project site. Carbon utilization can increase domestic supplies of traditional energy products such as oil as well as support the development of new fuels (such as innovative e-fuels), more efficient construction materials, and everyday consumer products. Figure 1 illustrates the capture, transport, and utilization processes.

Figure 1. Carbon Capture and Utilization

Source: ClearPath, “Carbon Utilization 101.” Available at: https://clearpath.org/tech-101/carbon-utilization-101/

Using Carbon Dioxide for Resource Extraction

Enhanced oil recovery (EOR) is one longstanding use of captured carbon to extract more oil from a reservoir. Carbon dioxide is injected into a well, moves through the pore space, and combines with drops of oil that cannot be pumped out through traditional means. The oil can then be extracted, with the carbon dioxide recycled for reuse. Applying EOR with carbon dioxide can result in net emissions reductions compared to conventional oil production as the injected carbon dioxide ultimately remains in the underground reservoir, a form of secure storage. This process can also be used to enhance natural gas recovery.

Figure 2. The Carbon Mineralization Process

Source: Bipartisan Policy Center, adapted from World Resources Institute, “What is Carbon Mineralization?,” June 22, 2023. Available at: https://www.wri.org/insights/carbon-mineralization-carbon-removal.

Carbon dioxide can also be used to both extract and recover critical minerals—a current focus area for Congress and the Trump administration. Carbon mineralization is a naturally occurring process in which carbon dioxide reacts with minerals inside certain types of rocks to create solid carbonates, as illustrated in Figure 2. Human intervention can accelerate this process by crushing up rocks to increase the surface area that comes in contact with carbon dioxide, allowing for greater quantities of carbon to be removed and stored while releasing critical minerals like nickel and cobalt as recoverable byproducts.

Carbon Dioxide as a Feedstock

Carbon dioxide can also be used as an input for a range of industrial and consumer products.

Figure 3. Uses for Captured Carbon Dioxide

The range of potential applications is broad, as illustrated in Figure 3, and includes the following:

Chemicals: Carbon dioxide can be used to produce polycarbonates—durable and transparent polymers typically used in electronics, eyeglasses, and automotive parts. Carbon dioxide can also diversify domestic polyurethane supply chains with carbon dioxide-based polyols. Polyurethane has a wide range of applications including foam, coating, and insulation.

Agriculture and Fertilizer: Mineral fertilizers are required to meet nearly 50% of global crop demand, and their production accounts for nearly 2% of global greenhouse gas emissions. Moreover, the fertilizer market can be vulnerable to global supply chain disruptions, with large amounts produced in the Middle East. Ammonia and urea fertilizer production utilize 125 million tons of carbon dioxide per year, representing a significant opportunity to incorporate captured carbon into existing industrial processes. In addition, carbon dioxide can directly enrich greenhouse environments to enhance plant growth and improve yields.

Concrete and Building Materials: The chemical reaction typically used to make cement, a powder ingredient required to make concrete, generates carbon dioxide as a byproduct. Cement production is a carbon dioxide intensive process, accounting for around 8% of global carbon emissions in 2022. Carbon dioxide, either captured carbon or the collected byproduct carbon dioxide, can be injected into concrete during the mixing process. The injected carbon dioxide reacts with ions present in the concrete mixture and forms a binding agent which enriches and strengthens the concrete. In 2023, Heirloom and CarbonCure launched a partnership where the captured carbon from Heirloom’s DAC facility is permanently embedded into concrete that is then used in construction projects.

E-fuels: E-fuels are low-carbon fuels synthesized from their chemical constituents (such as hydrogen, carbon dioxide, nitrogen) utilizing low- or zero-emissions energy sources. Carbon dioxide can be used as a feedstock for e-fuels such as sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), methanol, and synthetic diesel, which can be substituted for refined fossil fuels. Commercial airlines like United Airlines have inked deals to invest in DAC facilities in exchange for the option to create SAF from captured carbon dioxide.

Consumer products: Captured carbon can be used in the manufacture of a wide range of consumer products. By converting carbon dioxide into intermediate chemicals such as alcohols, acids, and polymers, innovators have produced everything from beer to shoes. While not necessarily scalable, the diversity of applications speaks to the versatility of carbon dioxide as a feedstock.

Federal Policy Support for Carbon Utilization

While the carbon utilization pathways described above show promise, many of them are in the nascent stage of development and/or require additional financial incentives to make them cost effective. Federal support for carbon capture and utilization is critical to advancing these technologies.

Carbon utilization received a boost with the passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA, Public Law 119-21) in 2025. In OBBBA, Congress modified section 45Q of the federal tax code, the carbon oxide sequestration tax credit, to provide parity for the storage and utilization of captured carbon. (The credit previously provided a higher value for carbon that was geologically sequestered.)

The federal government also provides support for carbon utilization R&D through a range of policies and programs. Most recently, the Department of Energy announced $36 million in federal funding for a new project to advance the commercial deployment of carbon dioxide-based EOR technologies. The Energy Act of 2020 also helped advance carbon utilization by authorizing DOE to assess novel uses for carbon dioxide and demonstrate carbon utilization technologies across industrial sectors. ARPA-E’s MINER initiative further advances this work by funding research into using carbon dioxide to unlock critical minerals.

Conclusion

Carbon utilization can support decarbonization while strengthening U.S. supply chains and energy security. DAC and other carbon capture and removal technologies are central to this value chain, providing a secure domestic supply of carbon dioxide. Supportive federal policy to help scale both the capture infrastructure and utilization applications will be necessary to fully realize these benefits.

text: At today’s APAC Sustainable Aviation Fuel conference in Melbourne, I highlighted the importance of transparent and robust book and claim mechanisms to connect supply with users across the Asia Pacific region. In the early days, SAF will be produced in a few regions, but there will be demand for it everywhere. So “book and claim” schemes distribute its benefits. Think of "book and claim" like buying green energy for your home: you pay for SAF to be produced, but you don't actually pump it into your specific flight. Because it will be concentrated at just a few places, shipping it everywhere would potentially create more carbon emissions than it saves. Instead, an airline "books" (pays for) a specific amount of SAF to be injected into the fuel system at an airport near the production facility, and then "claims" the environmental credit to meet their own sustainability commitments. Many nations allow this within their own jurisdictions - like Australia does with its safeguard mechanism. But this relies on distribution only within the country. We see the scope for partnerships - green lanes, bilateral or multilateral agreements between countries, to allow the claims to be made across borders. Operators in the Pacific Islands, for example, will have little ability to use locally produced SAF as their nations lack feedstock to produce. But they can benefit from production in places like Singapore, Japan, Australia and the like, if such schemes can be agreed. For example, for the first anniversary of the launch of its Nouméa–Paris (via Bangkok) route in December 2025, Aircalin derived the benefit of a Book and Claim transaction on the leg between Bangkok and Nouméa, where physical SAF was not available, but was paid for and physically uplifted elsewhere in Europe, where supply was available. Airbus has developed a Book and Claim Demonstrator to test the mechanisms, share the benefits and show the industry how it can work. To distribute the opportunities to use SAF around the region, such schemes have real merit when they can be agreed as part of national frameworks with like-minded countries, and the Asia Pacific region has many opportunities to build these frameworks. The mechanisms need to be robust and transparent to ensure confidence of users and customers. However, for it to work, we still need supply of SAF, which is why I reinforced the message of urgency - to get SAF production moving throughout our region - especially in the places where feedstock is ample, such as Australia.
